A (Introduction to Fields)

Words: 546 Articles: 9
2012 OurBigBook.com

A2

Words: 546 Articles: 8
A OurBigBook.com

a

Words: 107 Articles: 1
A2 OurBigBook.com
Solution
Words: 107
a OurBigBook.com
Start with O=(0,0) and E=(1,0). A constructible point is a point obtained from these by finitely many ruler-and-compass steps. At each step one may draw the line through two previously obtained distinct points, or the circle with a previously obtained centre and radius equal to the distance between two previously obtained points, and take isolated intersection points of the drawn lines or circles. A constructible line is a line through two distinct constructible points; a constructible circle has constructible centre and a radius obtainable as such a distance. These conventions also permit copying a previously obtained segment with the compass.
Finite construction from a fixed unit segment is essential: a drawing through an arbitrary unspecified real point does not make that point constructible.

b

Words: 191 Articles: 1
A2 OurBigBook.com
Solution
Words: 191
b OurBigBook.com
Consider an isolated intersection of the two curves. For two distinct lines, solving their linear equations by elimination gives coordinates in F whenever there is an intersection.
For a line and a circle, solve the line for one coordinate with a nonzero coefficient and substitute into the circle equation. The resulting quadratic has coefficients in F. A real root lies in F if its discriminant is a square in F, and otherwise in F(D​) for its positive nonsquare discriminant D∈F. The other coordinate is an F-linear expression in that root. Thus both coordinates lie in the same real quadratic extension. A tangent intersection has discriminant zero and already lies in F.
Write two circle equations in normalized form x2+y2+ui​x+vi​y+wi​=0. Subtracting eliminates the quadratic terms. If the circles are distinct and meet, this gives a nontrivial line, reducing the problem to the preceding case. Concentric distinct circles do not intersect. Therefore
each isolated intersection has coordinates in F or in F(D​),[F(D​):F]=2.​
(1)
The isolated-intersection qualification is implicit in the construction operation. If coincident curves were allowed and every point on their common curve counted as an intersection point, the printed assertion would be false: a rational line contains points with transcendental coordinates.

c

Words: 135 Articles: 1
A2 OurBigBook.com
Solution
Words: 135
c OurBigBook.com
Induct through the finitely many construction steps. Initially all available coordinates lie in Q. If coordinates obtained so far lie in a real field F, the line through two of its points has coefficients in F. A circle with centre in F2 and radius a distance between two such points has equation
(x−a)2+(y−b)2=r2,
(2)
whose coefficients lie in F, since the squared distance r2 lies in F; the radius itself need not lie there.
Part (b) therefore puts every new intersection in F or a real quadratic extension of F. If a step produces several points, adjoin their coordinates successively, omitting extensions that add nothing. A finite construction ends in a real field K containing the desired coordinates, with a tower of genuine quadratic extensions
Q=F0​⊂F1​⊂⋯⊂Fn​=K.
(3)
The tower law for field extensions yields
[K:Q]=i=0∏n−1​[Fi+1​:Fi​]=2n.​
(4)
A construction involving no nontrivial extension has n=0 and degree one.

d

Words: 113 Articles: 1
A2 OurBigBook.com
Solution
Words: 113
d OurBigBook.com
A constructible regular polygon can be translated, rotated, and rescaled by constructible operations to one inscribed in the unit circle with a vertex at (1,0). Thus the real and imaginary parts of ζ=e2πi/p are constructible. Part (c) puts both in a real field K of degree 2n over Q. Consequently ζ∈K(i), and [K(i):Q]=2n+1 because K⊂R.
For prime p, the supplied irreducibility of 1+x+⋯+xp−1 shows that [Q(ζ):Q]=p−1. The intermediate-field tower law implies that p−1 divides 2n+1. Every positive divisor of a power of two is a power of two, so
p=2r+1for an integer r≥0.​
(5)
This necessary condition includes p=2 with r=0. It does not assert sufficiency for arbitrary integers of this form.

The identity element satisfies e∗x=exe−1=x. For g,h∈G,
(gh)∗x=ghxh−1g−1=g∗(h∗x).
(6)
Both action axioms hold, so conjugation is a group action on G.

b

Words: 32 Articles: 1
B2 OurBigBook.com
Solution
Words: 32
b OurBigBook.com
By definition, g stabilizes x exactly when gxg−1=x. Multiplying on the right by g gives the equivalent condition gx=xg. Hence
StabG​(x)=Z(x).​
(7)
Thus the stabilizer in this action is the centralizer of the element.

c

Words: 64 Articles: 1
B2 OurBigBook.com
Solution
Words: 64
c OurBigBook.com
Let H=Z(x). The map G/H→C(x) sending gH to gxg−1 is well defined: multiplying g on the right by an element commuting with x leaves its conjugate unchanged. It is onto by the orbit definition. If gxg−1=hxh−1, then h−1g commutes with x, so gH=hH, proving injectivity.
Every coset has ∣H∣ elements, so ∣C(x)∣=∣G∣/∣H∣. Therefore
∣G∣=∣Z(x)∣∣C(x)∣.​
(8)
This is the orbit-stabilizer theorem specialized to conjugation.

d

Words: 64 Articles: 1
B2 OurBigBook.com
Solution
Words: 64
d OurBigBook.com
An element x is central exactly when gx=xg for every g∈G. By part (b), this is exactly the assertion that every g stabilizes x. That means every conjugate of x is x; conversely, a singleton conjugacy class has this property for every g.
x∈Z(G)⟺StabG​(x)=G⟺C(x)={x}.​
(9)
In particular, the singleton classes are in one-to-one correspondence with the elements of the centre.

e

Words: 40 Articles: 1
B2 OurBigBook.com
Solution
Words: 40
e OurBigBook.com
Conjugacy is an equivalence relation: the identity element gives reflexivity, conjugation by g−1 reverses conjugation by g, and composing conjugations gives transitivity. Its equivalence classes therefore partition the finite set G. Counting this disjoint union gives
∣G∣=i=1∑k​∣Ci​∣.​
(10)
Separating singleton classes from the others gives the class equation ∣G∣=∣Z(G)∣+∑∣Ci​∣>1​∣Ci​∣.

f

Words: 68 Articles: 1
B2 OurBigBook.com
Solution
Words: 68
f OurBigBook.com
Write ∣G∣=pn, where n≥1. By part (c), each conjugacy-class size divides pn and hence is a power of p. Every nonsingleton class consequently has size divisible by p. The class equation implies
∣Z(G)∣≡∣G∣≡0(modp).
(11)
The identity element lies in the centre, so the centre is nonempty. Its size is a positive multiple of p, and therefore
∣Z(G)∣≥p≥2.​
(12)
This proves that a nontrivial finite p-group has a nontrivial centre.

For an integer a and an odd prime p, the Legendre symbol is
(pa​)=⎩⎨⎧​0,1,−1,​p∣a,a≡0(modp) and a is a square modulo p,a is not a square modulo p.​​
(13)
The value one refers to a nonzero quadratic residue; divisibility by p is recorded separately by zero.

ii OurBigBook.com
Euler's criterion states that
a(p−1)/2≡(pa​)(modp).​
(14)
For p∤a this says that the power is 1 for a quadratic residue and −1 for a quadratic nonresidue. When p∣a, both sides are zero modulo p.
iii
Words: 72 Articles: 1
a OurBigBook.com
Solution
Words: 72
iii OurBigBook.com
Euler's criterion gives
(pab​)≡(ab)(p−1)/2≡a(p−1)/2b(p−1)/2≡(pa​)(pb​)(modp).
(15)
If either factor is divisible by p, both asserted values are zero. Otherwise the two values lie in {1,−1}, whose elements are distinct modulo an odd prime. The modular congruence is therefore equality:
(pab​)=(pa​)(pb​).​
(16)
Finally, a≡b(modp) means they give the same residue class and thus the same set of square-congruence solutions. Divisibility by p is also identical. Hence (pa​)=(pb​).

The quadratic reciprocity states that for distinct odd primes p,q,
(qp​)(pq​)=(−1)(p−1)(q−1)/4.
(17)
With q=3, it gives (p3​)=(−1)(p−1)/2(3p​). The nonzero square modulo three is one, so (3p​)=1 when p≡1(mod3), and −1 when p≡−1(mod3). An odd prime other than three is congruent to 1,5,7, or 11 modulo twelve. Evaluating the two signs gives
pmod12(−1)(p−1)/2(3p​)(p3​)​1111​51−1−1​7−11−1​11−1−11​​
(18)
Thus
(p3​)=1 for p≡±1(mod12),−1 for p≡±5(mod12).​
(19)

Reducing modulo 23 gives 189≡5. Reciprocity with five has positive sign, so
(23189​)=(235​)=(523​)=(53​)=−1,
(20)
since the nonzero squares modulo five are one and four. Modulo 59, 189≡12=4⋅3, and 59≡−1(mod12). Thus part (b) gives
(23189​)=−1,(59189​)=1.​
(21)
As 1357=23⋅59, a solution modulo 1357 would in particular solve the modular congruence modulo 23, contradicting the first symbol. Therefore there is no integer solution modulo 1357.

The monotone convergence theorem states that if measurable functions 0≤fn​↑f pointwise on a measure space, then ∫fn​↑∫f, allowing the limit to be infinite.
Extend each restriction to In​ by zero on I∖In​. The functions f1In​​ are nonnegative and increase pointwise to f because the intervals are increasing and exhaust I. Hence
∫I​f=limn→∞​∫In​​f=supn​∫In​​f.
(22)
For nonnegative f, integrability means finiteness of this integral, so
f∈L1(I)⟺nsup​∫In​​f<∞.​
(23)
No boundedness or closedness of the intervals is required.

0≤e2x+e−2xex+e−x​≤2e−∣x∣.

We prove absolute integrability. On (0,1], ∣sin(1/x)∣≤1 and the denominator is at least one, so ∣f(x)∣≤1. On [1,∞), the standard inequality ∣sint∣≤∣t∣ gives
∣f(x)∣≤x(1+(logx)2)1​.
(27)
Substitution t=logx yields
∫1∞​x(1+(logx)2)dx​=∫0∞​1+t2dt​=2π​.
(28)
Thus ∫0∞​∣f(x)∣dx≤1+π/2<∞, and the function is integrable despite its oscillation near zero.

Solution

D4 OurBigBook.com
For a continuously differentiable diffeomorphism ϕ:J→I between intervals, the integration by substitution states
∫I​h(x)dx=∫J​h(ϕ(t))∣ϕ′(t)∣dt.
(29)
It holds as an identity element of extended integrals for nonnegative measurable h. For signed or complex-valued measurable h, integrability on one side is equivalent to integrability after substitution, and the identity element then holds. The absolute derivative accounts for a decreasing substitution; on oriented finite intervals the equivalent formula uses ϕ′ and oriented endpoints.
Put C=∫0∞​(1+x4)−1dx=π/(22​). The map x=y−1/4 is a decreasing diffeomorphism of the positive half-line onto itself and
1+x4∣dx/dy∣​=4y1/4(1+y)1​.
(30)
Applying the nonnegative version before assuming finiteness proves both existence and value:
∫0∞​y1/4(1+y)dy​=4C=2​π.​
(31)
Tonelli's theorem permits either iterated integral of a nonnegative measurable function on a product of sigma-finite measure spaces and identifies both with its extended product integral. Fubini's theorem states that for an absolutely integrable measurable function on such a product, almost every section is integrable, the section-integral functions are integrable, and the two iterated integrals equal the product integral.
The given two-variable function is continuous and positive on the positive quadrant. For fixed y>0, substituting t=xy1/4 gives
∫0∞​f(x,y)dx=1+yCy−1/4​.
(32)
Tonelli now gives
∬f(x,y)dxdy=C(4C)=4C2=2π2​<∞.
(33)
This proves absolute integrability, so Fubini is applicable.
For x=1, integrate the displayed partial fraction identity element in y up to R:
∫0R​f(x,y)dy=x4−1log(1+x4R)−log(1+R)​⟶x4−14logx​.
(34)
At x=1 the section integral is ∫0∞​(1+y)−2dy=1, agreeing with the continuous limit of this expression. Therefore Fubini identifies the remaining integral and gives
∫0∞​x4−1logx​dx=41​⋅2π2​=8π2​.​
(35)
The apparent singularity at one is removable, with limiting integrand value 1/4. Positivity and the finite product integral already establish convergence at both ends.

i OurBigBook.com
The closure of A is the intersection of every closed subset containing it:
A=⋂{F⊆X:F closed and A⊆F}.​
(36)
The collection is nonempty because it contains X. Arbitrary intersections of closed sets are closed, so this is the smallest closed set containing A.
ii
Words: 55 Articles: 1
a OurBigBook.com
Solution
Words: 55
ii OurBigBook.com
Every subset is contained in its closure, giving A⊆A. On the other hand, A is already closed by its definition as an intersection of closed sets. It is therefore one of the closed supersets used when taking its own closure, so A⊆A. Hence
A=A.​
(37)
This is the idempotence of the closure operation.
iii
Words: 61 Articles: 1
a OurBigBook.com
Solution
Words: 61
iii OurBigBook.com
If x∈/A, some closed superset F of A misses x. Its complement is an open set containing x and disjoint from A. Conversely, if an open set U contains x and misses A, the closed set X∖U contains A and misses x, so x∈/A.
Negating this equivalence gives the neighbourhood characterization
x∈A⟺U∩A=∅ for every open U∋x.​
(38)

Words: 52 Articles: 1

Solution

iv OurBigBook.com
An accumulation point of A is a point x∈X such that every open neighbourhood of x contains a point of A different from x:
x∈A′⟺(U∖{x})∩A=∅ for every open U∋x.​
(39)
The point itself need not belong to A. Requiring a different point distinguishes accumulation from mere membership in the closure.

Take A1​=Q2. Every open disk contains infinitely many points with both coordinates rational, so every point of the plane is an accumulation point of A1​. Every disk also contains infinitely many points with an irrational first coordinate, and these lie in the complement. Thus
A1′​=R2=(R2∖A1​)′.​
(41)
The infinitely-many-points observation ensures that one can avoid the centre of the disk itself in both cases.

Solution
Words: 64
2 OurBigBook.com
Take
A2​={(1/n,0):n≥1}.
(42)
Its only accumulation point is (0,0), which is absent from A2​. Every listed point is isolated, so none belongs to A2′​. Consequently
A2′​={(0,0)},A2′​⊆A2​,A2​⊆A2′​.​
(43)
For completeness, away from the origin a sufficiently small disk meets only finitely many of the listed points and can be shrunk to exclude all but its centre, proving there are no further accumulation points.
3
Words: 171 Articles: 1
ii OurBigBook.com
Solution
Words: 171
3 OurBigBook.com
Use three nested sequences:
A3​={(n1​+n2m1​,n2m2k1​):n,m,k≥1}.
(44)
For fixed n,m, letting k→∞ produces the point (1/n+1/(n2m),0). Letting m→∞ produces (1/n,0), and letting n→∞ produces (0,0). Accordingly, put
B={(n1​+n2m1​,0):n,m≥1},C={(1/n,0):n≥1}.
(45)
The successive derived sets are
A3′​=B∪C∪{(0,0)},A3′′​=C∪{(0,0)},A3′′′​={(0,0)}.​
(46)
To see that no limits are missing, take any convergent sequence of distinct points from A3​. If n is unbounded, a subsequence has n→∞ and converges to the origin. Otherwise fix n on a subsequence. Unbounded m then forces limit (1/n,0); with n,m fixed, distinctness forces unbounded k, giving the corresponding point of B. The same argument, with one index fewer at each stage, proves the next two equalities. Distinct n-clusters are separated away from the origin because their first coordinates lie in the disjoint intervals [1/n,1/n+1/n2].
The original set has positive second coordinates, the first derived set has isolated B-points on the axis, the second has infinitely many C-points, and the third is a singleton. All three required successive inequalities follow. This is a three-stage accumulation tower.

Since the first-coordinate difference in a−gnb grows without bound as ∣n∣→∞, the positive distances d(a,gnb) have a positive minimum δ. Only finitely many indices can give a distance below any fixed bound, and none gives zero.
Choose 0<ε<δ/3. Saturate the relative open balls by setting

Two representatives in D are in the same orbit only if their first coordinates differ by an integer. An interior point can therefore be equivalent only to itself. Distinct boundary representatives have first coordinates zero and one, and the iterate g identifies exactly (0,y) with (1,−y). Thus the fibres of q are precisely the equivalence classes defining the Möbius band M.
The rectangle D is compact, and the target is Hausdorff by part (i). Applying part (a)(v) to q therefore yields
M=D/R≅S/R′.​

Take a smooth variation u+εv with v=0 on the boundary. Differentiating under the integral gives the first variation
δI[u](v)=∬R​(Fu​v+Fuξ​​vξ​+Fuζ​​vζ​)dξdζ.
(64)
Integration by parts removes the derivatives of v, and the boundary contribution vanishes. The fundamental lemma of the calculus of variations therefore gives
Fu​−∂ξ​Fuξ​​−∂ζ​Fuζ​​=0.​
(65)
For a regular constraint J[u]=c, the Lagrange multiplier rule says that an extremal satisfies δI=λδJ for a constant λ. Equivalently, apply the preceding Euler–Lagrange equation to F−λG. Regularity means that δJ is not identically zero as a linear functional on the admissible variations. For the quadratic constraint below this holds at every nonzero admissible u; a zero constraint leaves only u=0.
In polar coordinates the constrained integrand is
L=rur2​+r1​uθ2​−λru2.
(66)
Its Euler–Lagrange equation is −2λru−∂r​(2rur​)−∂θ​(2uθ​/r)=0, or
urr​+r1​ur​+r21​uθθ​+λu=0,u(a,θ)=0.​
(67)
The field is single-valued and periodic in θ. Substitution u=f(r)cos(nθ) with n∈{0,1,2,…} gives
f′′+r1​f′+(λ−r2n2​)f=0,f(a)=0.​
(68)
The centre is part of the disk, so one must also select the regular radial solution: for n≥1, smoothness gives f(r)=O(rn) and the regular derivative behaviour; for n=0, f is bounded and f′(0)=0. A singular solution at zero does not define an admissible smooth field on the disk.
For fixed n, let cn​=∫02π​cos2(nθ)dθ, so c0​=2π and cn​=π for n≥1. The angular derivative term has integral n2cn​, including zero when n=0. Consequently
I[f]=cn​∫0a​(rf′2+rn2​f2)dr,J[f]=cn​∫0a​rf2dr.
(69)
The one-dimensional Euler–Lagrange equation for I−λJ is
−(rf′)′+rn2​f=λrf,
(70)
exactly the same radial equation. The common factor cn​ cancels.
For two regular solutions with the same n and different multipliers, multiply the equation for f1​ by f2​, multiply that for f2​ by f1​, subtract and integrate. The result is
(λ1​−λ2​)∫0a​rf1​f2​dr=[r(f1​f2′​−f1′​f2​)]0a​=0.
(71)
At a, both functions vanish; at zero, regularity makes the boundary term tend to zero. Since the multipliers are distinct,
∫0a​rf1​f2​dr=0.​
(72)
This is weighted Sturm–Liouville orthogonality with weight r.
Finally, multiply one radial equation by f and integrate by parts. The same endpoint conditions yield
∫0a​(rf′2+rn2​f2)dr=λ∫0a​rf2dr.
(73)
Multiplication by cn​ proves
I[fi​]−λi​J[fi​]=0.​
(74)
For any nonzero admissible solution the energy on the left before subtraction is positive, so its multiplier is the positive Rayleigh quotient λ=I/J.

Convergence at a jump of FY​ is not required. Only the laws are involved, so this definition does not require a particular coupling of the variables.

Assume convergence in probability and fix ε>0. On the event ∣Yn​−Y∣≤ε, Y≤x−ε implies Yn​≤x, while Yn​≤x implies Y≤x+ε. Hence
FY​(x−ε)−P(∣Yn​−Y∣>ε)≤FYn​​(x)≤FY​(x+ε)+P(∣Yn​−Y∣>ε).
(123)
Taking lower and upper limits in n removes the error probabilities. If x is a continuity point of FY​, letting ε↓0 squeezes both bounds to FY​(x). Thus
Yn​→Y in probability⟹Yn​→Y in distribution.​
(124)

Solution

M5 OurBigBook.com
A homogeneous Poisson process of rate λ>0 is an integer-valued counting process with N0​=0 almost surely, nondecreasing right-continuous paths with unit jumps, and independent stationary increments satisfying
Nt​−Ns​∼Poisson(λ(t−s)),0≤s<t.​
(125)
Increments over disjoint time intervals are independent. In particular,
P(Nt​=k)=e−λtk!(λt)k​,k=0,1,2,….
(126)
The finite Poisson counts ensure that there is no explosion in finite time. The increment formula also gives stochastic continuity, since the probability of any arrival in an interval of length h is 1−e−λh→0.

Since N3​∼Poisson(3λ),
P(N3​≥1)=1−P(N3​=0)=1−e−3λ.​
(127)

Stationary increments give N5​−N3​∼Poisson(2λ). Therefore
P(N5​−N3​=4)=e−2λ4!(2λ)4​.​
(128)
There is zero probability of an arrival at either deterministic endpoint, so endpoint inclusion does not alter the result.

c OurBigBook.com
Successive interarrival times W1​=T1​ and W2​=T2​−T1​ are independent exponential variables of rate λ. Their joint density is λ2e−λ(w1​+w2​) for w1​,w2​>0. The transformation t1​=w1​, t2​=w1​+w2​ has Jacobian determinant one, giving
fT1​,T2​​(t1​,t2​)=λ2e−λt2​1{0<t1​<t2​}​.​
(129)
Integrating over 0<t1​<t2​<∞ gives one, as a joint density should.

Solution

d OurBigBook.com
Write N3​=N2​+(N3​−N2​). Independent increments make N2​ independent of the second term. Hence
Cov(N2​,N3​)=Var(N2​)=2λ.​
(130)
The overlapping time interval contributes the covariance; the extra unit of time contributes none.

e

Words: 97 Articles: 1
M5 OurBigBook.com
Solution
Words: 97
e OurBigBook.com
After the third arrival, the future interarrival times are independent of the first three interarrival times and again generate a rate-λ Poisson process. Conditional on T3​=t<2, exactly three arrivals have occurred by time t, and the number of further arrivals before two is Poisson with mean λ(2−t). Consequently, in the regular conditional-distribution sense at t=1,
N2​∣(T3​=1) ∼ 3+Poisson(λ).​
(131)
Explicitly its conditional mass is zero for k<3 and is
P(N2​=k∣T3​=1)=e−λ(k−3)!λk−3​,k≥3.
(132)
This conditions on the third arrival time itself, rather than merely on the event that the third arrival has happened by time one.

For the shifted exponential model, F(x)=1−e−λ(x−1) for x≥1. It is increasing, so the probability integral transform preserves order: F(X(r)​)=Y(r)​. The expected uniform plotting positions are r/(n+1) by part (b). Replacing the random transformed order statistic by this representative position gives
1−e−λ(x(r)​−1)≈n+1r​,x(r)​≈1+λ1​[−log(1−n+1r​)].

Thus plotting x(r)​ against tr​=−log(1−r/(n+1)) should give an approximate line with intercept one and slope 1/λ​.
The replacement is a quantile-plot approximation, not an assertion that expectation commutes exactly with the nonlinear inverse distribution function. The random points need not lie exactly on the line.

For the Pareto model, integration gives F(x)=1−x−λ on x≥1. The same plotting positions suggest 1−x(r)−λ​≈r/(n+1). Taking logarithms gives
logx(r)​≈λ1​[−log(1−n+1r​)].

Therefore plot logx(r)​ vertically against tr​=−log(1−r/(n+1)) horizontally. A reasonable fit should be approximately a straight line through the origin, with slope 1/λ​. This logarithmic transformation distinguishes the Pareto tail model from the shifted exponential plot in part (i).

Independence and normality give X∼N(μ,1/n). Consequently Z=n​(X−μ) is standard normal, and
P(X<μ+n​zα​​)=Φ(zα​)=1−α.
(142)
Rearranging the event gives μ>X−zα​/n​. Thus the random interval (X−zα​/n​,∞) covers the fixed parameter with probability 1−α. After observing the sample, its realized confidence interval is
(x−n​zα​​,∞).​
(143)
The coverage refers to repeated samples, not to a posterior probability for the fixed parameter.

b

Solution
Words: 89
b OurBigBook.com
The Neyman-Pearson lemma concerns testing two simple hypotheses with densities f0​ and f1​ relative to a common measure. A test that rejects when f1​(x)>kf0​(x), accepts when f1​(x)<kf0​(x), and randomizes on equality if necessary to achieve size α, is most powerful among all tests with size at most α:
E0​φ=α⟹E1​ψ≤E1​φ for every test ψ with E0​ψ≤α.​
(144)
Here φ is the described likelihood-ratio test and test functions take values in [0,1]. In the continuous normal setting below the boundary has probability zero, so randomization is unnecessary.

The likelihood ratio between the two normal means is
L(μ0​;x)L(μ1​;x)​=exp((μ1​−μ0​)∑i=1n​xi​−2n​(μ12​−μ02​)).
(145)
Since μ1​>μ0​, it is strictly increasing in x. The Neyman–Pearson test therefore rejects for large sample means. Under the null, n​(X−μ0​)∼N(0,1), so choosing a right-tail probability α gives
cα​=μ0​+n​zα​​,C={x:x≥cα​}.​
(146)
This has size exactly α because the sampling distribution is continuous.

For every particular alternative mean μ1​>μ0​, the likelihood ratio is increasing in the same statistic x. Its size-α threshold is fixed solely by the null distribution, so it is always the same cα​ found in part (c), independent of μ1​.
The single rejection region is therefore most powerful against every member of the composite alternative. Hence the test is uniformly most powerful for H1​:μ>μ0​.

A real square matrix Q is orthogonal when QTQ=I, equivalently Q−1=QT. For c=cosθ and s=sinθ,
M(θ)TM(θ)=(cs​−sc​)(c−s​sc​)=(c2+s20​0c2+s2​)=I.
(151)
Thus M(θ) is orthogonal for every allowed angle, and indeed for every real angle.

Using orthogonality,
∥Qx∥2=(Qx)TQx=xTQTQx=xTx=∥x∥2.
(152)
Both norms are nonnegative, so taking square roots proves
∥Qx∥=∥x∥.​
(153)
Thus an orthogonal matrix is a Euclidean isometry fixing the origin.

c

Words: 95 Articles: 1

Solution
Words: 95
c OurBigBook.com
The columns outside indices i,j are unchanged coordinate vectors. The remaining two columns have nonzero entries only in rows i,j, with the 2×2 block M(θ). They have squared norm cos2θ+sin2θ=1 and mutual inner product zero; they are also orthogonal to all the unchanged columns. Hence JTJ=I.
Let r=xi2​+xj2​​. If r>0, choose θ∈[−π,π] with cosθ=xi​/r and sinθ=xj​/r. Then
yi​=cosθxi​+sinθxj​=r,yj​=−sinθxi​+cosθxj​=0.
(154)
Every other coordinate is unchanged. If r=0, choose θ=0; the same conclusions hold. Therefore the procedure can be fixed with the nonnegative pivot convention
yi​=xi2​+xj2​​,yj​=0,yk​=xk​ (k=i,j).​
(155)
This is a Givens rotation.

d

Words: 206 Articles: 1
P3 OurBigBook.com
Solution
Words: 206
d OurBigBook.com
Write J1​,J2​,J3​ for the actual successive rotations J(1,2), J(1,3), and J(2,3), each selected using the currently transformed matrix. The first eliminates position (2,1); the second eliminates (3,1) while leaving row two unchanged. After these, the first column is (r11​,0,0)T. The final rotation of rows two and three preserves both zeros in that column and eliminates (3,2). Hence
R=J3​J2​J1​A is upper triangular.​
(156)
A lower-triangular starting matrix does not force any further zeros above the diagonal. For example, the lower-triangular matrix with all entries on and below its diagonal equal to one gives, with the nonnegative pivot convention,
R=​3​00​2/3​2/3​0​1/3​1/6​1/2​​​,
(157)
which has all upper-triangular entries nonzero.
Inverting the product of rotations yields the QR factorization
Q=J1T​J2T​J3T​,A=QR.​
(158)
The order reverses when taking the transpose. If A is orthogonal, then R is both orthogonal and upper triangular. Its first column forces ∣r11​∣=1 and orthogonality with the other columns forces r12​=r13​=0. Applying the same argument to the remaining block makes R diagonal with entries of modulus one.
Our elimination rule makes r11​ and r22​ positive when nonzero, so they are both one. Every rotation has determinant one; thus detR=detA and
R=diag(1,1,detA).​
(159)
Without a fixed pivot-sign convention one could only specify a diagonal sign matrix. The convention chosen in part (c) determines the precise signs above.

by Pascal's identity; the two endpoint coefficients agree as well. Therefore
Q(r)​(x)−Q(r)​(x−h)=Q(r+1)​(x).​

For a degree-d polynomial with leading coefficient c=0, the backward difference has leading term

Since h>0, this coefficient is nonzero for d≥1. Starting with Q(0)​=P, iteration gives degree n−r and leading coefficient chrn!/(n−r)! for 0≤r≤n. The next difference of the resulting constant is zero:
degQ(r)​=n−r (0≤r≤n),Q(n+1)​≡0.​

b OurBigBook.com
A natural cubic spline with the given knots is a C2 function that is polynomial of degree at most three on each interval between consecutive knots and has S′′(x0​)=S′′(x4​)=0. With the usual whole-line convention, it extends affinely outside the extreme knots. The word natural refers to these endpoint second-derivative conditions; the interpolation values must be specified separately.
For Hk​(x)=(x−xk​)+3​, direct differentiation on either side of the knot gives
Hk′​(x)=3(x−xk​)+2​,Hk′′​(x)=6(x−xk​)+​.
(164)
Both one-sided limits of the function and its first two derivatives at xk​ are zero, so these formulas are continuous there and
Hk​∈C2(R).​
(165)
Its third derivative jumps from zero to six, which is permitted for a cubic spline.

c

Solution

c OurBigBook.com
The finite sum of truncated cubes is C2 by part (b) and is cubic on each knot interval. For x≤0, every term vanishes. For x≥4h, every truncated power equals its ordinary polynomial, so part (a) applied to P(x)=x3 gives
S(3)​(x)=∑k=04​(−1)k(k4​)(x−kh)3=Q(4)​(x)=0.
(166)
It is therefore zero on both exterior intervals. Its C2 regularity makes the endpoint second derivatives zero too, proving naturality.
Evaluation at the five knots gives
(S(3)​(0),S(3)​(h),S(3)​(2h),S(3)​(3h),S(3)​(4h))=h3(0,1,4,1,0).​
(167)
For example the three interior values in units of h3 are 1, 8−4=4, and 27−4⋅8+6=1. At 4h the cancellation is 64−4⋅27+6⋅8−4=0.
For h=1 an explicit graph description is
S(3)​(x)=⎩⎨⎧​0,x3,4−6(x−2)2+3∣x−2∣3,(4−x)3,​x≤0 or x≥4,0≤x≤1,1≤x≤3,3≤x≤4.​
(168)
It is symmetric about x=2, increases from zero to its maximum four at the centre, and decreases symmetrically back to zero. It joins the zero tails with zero first and second derivatives.
